chmmc-2012-fall-mixer-01.title: Monotonic function
chmmc-2012-fall-mixer-01.body: Dividing by $5^x$, the equation becomes $\left(\frac35\right)^x+\left(\frac45\right)^x=1$. The left side $g(x)$ is strictly decreasing (both bases are in $(0,1)$) and $g(2)=\frac9{25}+\frac{16}{25}=1$. A strictly decreasing function takes each value at most once, so $x=2$ is the only solution. $\blacksquare$

chmmc-2012-fall-mixer-02.title: Square it
chmmc-2012-fall-mixer-02.body: Let $E$ be the expression; $E>0$ and $E^2=(9+4\sqrt5)+(9-4\sqrt5)-2\sqrt{81-80}=18-2=16$, so $E=4$. $\blacksquare$

chmmc-2012-fall-mixer-03.title: Symmetry strategy
chmmc-2012-fall-mixer-03.body: $A$ puts the first coin exactly at the center $O$ of the table. Whenever $B$ places a coin with center $P$, $A$ answers with the coin centered at the reflection $P'$ of $P$ in $O$. This is always legal. It is on the table by symmetry. It does not overlap the center coin: $|OP'|=|OP|\ge2r$ since $B$'s coin did not overlap it ($r$ is the coin radius). It does not overlap $B$'s new coin, since $|PP'|=2|OP|\ge4r>2r$. It does not overlap an older coin $Q$: the set of older coins is symmetric about $O$ (the center coin and mirror pairs), and $P'$ overlapping $Q$ would mean $P$ overlaps the mirror image of $Q$, an older coin, which $B$'s legal move did not. So $A$ always has a reply; the game is finite, so it is $B$ who eventually cannot move. $A$ wins. $\blacksquare$

chmmc-2012-fall-mixer-04.title: Lattice invariant
chmmc-2012-fall-mixer-04.body:
Scale so the pegs start at $(0,0),(1,0),(0,1),(1,1)$. Reflecting $P$ through $Q$ gives $2Q-P$. Let $\Lambda$ be the lattice generated by all differences of peg positions; initially $\Lambda=\mathbb Z^2$. After a move, the new differences are $(2Q-P)-R=(Q-P)+(Q-R)$ and $(2Q-P)-Q=Q-P$, all in $\Lambda$, so $\Lambda'\subseteq\Lambda$; the move can be undone by the same move, so $\Lambda'=\Lambda$. A square with vertices $V,V+v,V+w,V+v+w$ ($w$ = $v$ rotated by $90^\circ$) generates the lattice $\mathbb Zv+\mathbb Zw$ of index $|v|^2$ in $\mathbb Z^2$. Since this must equal $\mathbb Z^2$, $|v|^2=1$, so every reachable square has side $1$: never larger. The answer is $0$.

**Answer: 0**

chmmc-2012-fall-mixer-05.title: CRT
chmmc-2012-fall-mixer-05.body:
$n\equiv-1\pmod2,\ -1\pmod3$ so $n\equiv-1\pmod6$; $n\equiv3\pmod5$ and $n\equiv5\pmod7$, i.e. $n\equiv-2\pmod7$. From $n=6k-1$: $6k-1\equiv3\pmod5\Rightarrow k\equiv4\pmod5$, so $n=30j+23$. Then $30j+23\equiv5\pmod7$: $2j+2\equiv5$, $j\equiv5\pmod7$ ($2j\equiv3$, $j\equiv5$). So $n=30\cdot5+23=173$ (the next is $383$).

**Answer: 173**

chmmc-2012-fall-mixer-06.title: Perfect number
chmmc-2012-fall-mixer-06.body:
$\sum_{m\mid496}\frac1m=\frac1{496}\sum_{m\mid 496}\frac{496}{m}=\frac{\sigma(496)}{496}$. Since $496=2^4\cdot31$, $\sigma(496)=31\cdot32=992=2\cdot496$ (it is a perfect number). The sum is $2$.

**Answer: 2**

chmmc-2012-fall-mixer-08.title: Structure of sweet sequences
chmmc-2012-fall-mixer-08.body:
Let $n=2014$ and $z=a_0$, the number of zeros. Every term is counted once, so $\sum a_i=n$. Also $a_0\ge1$ (if $a_0=0$ then $0$ would not appear, but $a_0$ itself is $0$). There are $n-z$ nonzero terms with sum $n$, so $\sum_{a_i\ne0}(a_i-1)=z$. The term $a_0=z$ already contributes $z-1$, so the other nonzero terms contribute excess exactly $1$: one of them is $2$ and all the rest equal $1$. Hence the sequence consists of $z$ zeros, the term $z$ at index $0$, one $2$, and $n-z-2$ ones. The number of $2$s is then $a_2=1$, and the number of $1$s is $a_1=n-z-2$. The single $2$ must sit at index $1$ (index $2$ holds a $1$, and a $2$ at another index $j$ would require the value $j$ to occur twice, impossible), so $a_1=2$ and $z=n-4=2010$; then the value $2010$ occurs once, at index $0$, so $a_{2010}=1$. Thus $a_0=2010$, $a_1=2$, $a_2=1$, $a_{2010}=1$, all others $0$, and $\sum a_i^2=2010^2+4+1+1=4040106$.

**Answer: 4040106**

chmmc-2012-fall-mixer-08.title: Check
chmmc-2012-fall-mixer-08.body:
Indeed with $a_0=2010,a_1=2,a_2=1,a_{2010}=1$ and all other $a_i=0$: the number of $0$s is $2014-4=2010$, the number of $1$s is $2$ ($a_2$ and $a_{2010}$), the number of $2$s is $1$, and the number of $2010$s is $1$. The squares sum to $2010^2+4+1+1=4040106$.

**Answer: 4040106**
